ety.text: From Middle English occupacioun, borrowed from Middle French occupacion, occupation, from Latin occupātiō, occupātiōnis, from occupō (“occupy, seize”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to seize, grab”). By surface analysis, occupy + -ation.

The act, process or state of possessing a place.

ex: The early years of Norman occupation saw a frenzy of castle building.

senses.d: To live or reside in.

senses.d: To have, or to have taken, possession or control of (a territory).
